summary:
SPHEREx Blink Tree is a public web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx sky survey into a short film of any patch of sky. You type coordinates or an object name; the tool finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s archive, reads only the pixels it needs, aligns them, stacks them visit by visit and plays them in a loop. Anything that moves or changes brightness stands out, and a difference view removes everything that stays the same.

It covers the challenge and its optional goals: six detector bands shown separately or combined, a selectable field of view, Gaia star overlays, quality flags, a sky map of all 102 SPHEREx channels, shareable links, and a spectrum and light curve for any star with one click. All five test targets work, including the brown dwarf WISE 0855. Nothing is pre-computed, so new weekly data appear automatically.

SPHEREx will image more than a billion objects, far too many for any one team to sift through. This tool lets volunteers, students and researchers search that data for new brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets and variable stars from a browser, in English or Turkish.
details:
What it does
SPHEREx Blink Tree is a web page that shows how any patch of sky changes over time in NASA’s SPHEREx survey. You enter coordinates or an object name; the tool lines up every SPHEREx visit of that spot and plays them as a short film. Four numbered boxes lead from a sky map, to the film, to the settings, to a spectrum and light curve of any star you click.

How it works
A small Python server asks NASA’s archive (IRSA) which SPHEREx images contain the position, which takes 1–5 seconds. Each image is a 62–66 MB file; the server reads only the rows around the target with HTTP range requests from the public copy on AWS, about 0.4 MB per file for a 3′ field. It aligns the windows north-up, groups exposures into visits, and stacks each detector with outlier rejection. The browser receives raw frames and does the blinking, difference, sum and contrast itself, so the controls respond instantly. Because SPHEREx sees a star at a different wavelength in every exposure, measuring a clicked star in all exposures gives its 0.75–5 µm spectrum and a light curve.

What it shows on the test targets
Barnard’s Star moves about 10″ per year. WISE 0855 appears only in the 4.4–5 µm detector and leaves a dark–bright pair in the difference view. Epsilon Indi B shows the water and methane bands of a brown dwarf. RW Aurigae faded to about half at 4–5 µm within a year. R Draconis saturates the detector, so the tool follows the light in a ring around it.

Benefits and intended impact
SPHEREx images more than a billion objects. The tool lets volunteers, students and researchers look for moving and variable objects from a browser, with nothing to install. Nothing is pre-computed, so new weekly data appear automatically, and every view is a link that can be shared or embedded.

Tools
Python (FastAPI, Uvicorn, astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Requests); plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Aladin Lite for the sky map. Data: SPHEREx images and all-sky maps from IRSA, Gaia DR3 from ESA, names from SIMBAD. The code and the report were developed with an AI coding assistant (Claude).

Creativity
Spectra without a spectrograph, built on the fly from the images. A sky map of all 102 channels with the footprints of the exposures. Ring photometry for stars too bright for the detector. SPHEREx’s quality flags explained in plain words. An offline demo that runs without the server, and an interface in English and Turkish.

What we considered
Speed: only the needed bytes are read, and results are cached. Trust: positions agree with Gaia DR3 to 0.4–0.8″ (median) and brightness with 2MASS to within about 6%; the limits of the quick-look photometry are stated. Reliability: when the archive’s search is down the tool works from earlier lists. Upkeep: a new data release is one line in a settings file.
